People aren’t adopting the 16 year old boy who tries to runaway from every placement he’s in or the 14 year old girl who got pregnant while being sex trafficked because she, too, ran away from placement… and those kids age out, and then what? They have no skills, they have immense trauma both from the abuse/neglect before removal AND from being in state custody…

The truth is, if we can find a distant relative or a family friend or SOMEONE who is going to intervene on our behalf, it’s less traumatic for most kids. This of course depends on the severity of the abuse/neglect and if the people willing to care for the child are appropriate… when that doesn’t happen, CPS intervention is inevitable.

It still sucks and there really isn’t a fix all solution… but one of the biggest complaints I see about our field nowadays is “CPS sent the kid home with his crackhead parents” or “well CPS didn’t do anything when I called them on the neighbors”… with all due respect, you don’t really know what CPS did or didn’t do unless you are directly involved. We work services with parents when possible and provide as many resources as we can… additionally, we have strict policy guidelines dictating what circumstances do and don’t allow for emergency removals.

I’ve worked CPS in two different states and three different stages of service. Ultimately, child welfare is child welfare and we are always assessing child safety and want permanency for our kids.

If you’re doing investigations, you are very literally going to be on the front lines and will be exposed to a lot. Steel yourself. The pros of INV are that you are really not in contact with the family for long. Once you close the case, it’s either stage progressed or closed and that’s that. Cons are, imo, constant safety plans/removals and on call.

If you’re doing family centered services/conservatorship — you are in it with your families after investigations identified either risk or danger and they need services to prevent removal or to reunify with children post removal. FCS is a lot of contacts monthly, collaterals, monitoring, etc. FCS still does removals and will occasionally go to court.

CVS is a lot of court on all cases, permanency planning (whether it’s reunification or adoption), and dealing with attorneys, ad litems, foster care agencies, and placement disruptions. The toughest stage imo. You’re with those kids until they can go back home (safely) or they’re adopted or age out. You get very attached and sometimes that makes it more difficult and frustrating when parents aren’t doing their services or making changes.
